# 1. Overview

This script combines field observation data collected across multiple years
in the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta into a single, standardized dataset.

Because the data were collected in different years, some columns have different
names even though they contain the same information. In addition, some columns
use different values or categories to describe the same observations.

The main goals of this script are to:

1. Identify columns that contain the same information but have different names.
2. Combine equivalent columns into a single column with a consistent name.
3. Standardize values within columns so the same categories and codes are used
   across all years.
4. Combine the individual shapefiles into a single dataset.
5. Save the cleaned dataset for future analyses.

**Important:** The original shapefiles are treated as raw data and should
never be modified or overwritten. All corrections are performed in R, and
the cleaned dataset is saved separately.

Set the default options for displaying code when the R Markdown file is
knitted into an HTML document.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# Display R code in the knitted document
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```


# 3. Load Required Packages

The following packages are needed to run this script.

If a package is not already installed on your computer, R will automatically
install it. Packages that are already installed will not be reinstalled.

```{r libraries, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# List of packages needed for this script
packages = c("terra", "tidyterra", "dplyr", "kableExtra",
             "openxlsx", "stringr")

# Identify packages that are not installed
missing_packages = packages[!packages %in% rownames(installed.packages())]

# Install missing packages, if any
if (length(missing_packages) > 0) {
  install.packages(missing_packages)
}

# Load all required packages
invisible(lapply(packages, library, character.only = TRUE))
```


# 4. Data Preparation

This section identifies the original shapefiles that will be used in the
analysis and separates point and line datasets.

The point shapefiles contain the field observations that will be combined
and standardized in this script.

## 4.1 Set Input and Output Locations

First, specify where the original shapefiles are stored and where the
cleaned datasets will be saved.

- `input_dir`: Folder containing the original, unmodified shapefiles.
- `outpath`: Folder where cleaned datasets and other outputs will be saved.
- `output_path1`: File location for the cleaned Excel dataset.
- `output_path2`: File location for the data-cleaning change log.

**Note:** Update these paths if running the script on a different computer.

```{r}
# Folder containing the ORIGINAL shapefiles (do not modify these files)
input_dir = "C:/Users/bdmor/Box/NASA-IAV/classification/data/model_inputs/shapefiles/CSTARS_All_FieldData/raw/"

# Folder where cleaned datasets will be saved
outpath = "C:/Users/bdmor/Box/NASA-IAV/classification/data/model_inputs/shapefiles/CSTARS_All_FieldData/"
```


## 4.2 Find All Shapefiles

The original data are stored as shapefiles (`.shp`), which contain spatial
features (points or lines) and their associated attribute data.

The code below searches the input folder and all its subfolders for shapefiles.

The resulting `files` object contains the full file path for every shapefile
found.

```{r}
# Find all shapefiles in the input directory and its subfolders
files = list.files(
  path = input_dir,
  pattern = "\\.shp$",
  full.names = TRUE,
  recursive = TRUE,
  ignore.case = TRUE
)

# Display the total number of shapefiles found
print(paste("Found", length(files), "shapefiles"))
```

## 4.3 Separate Point and Line Shapefiles

The field data contain both point and line shapefiles.

- **Point shapefiles:** Individual locations where field observations were
  collected.
- **Line shapefiles:** Spatial features represented by lines.

These datasets need to be processed separately because they contain
different types of spatial features.

The filenames and folder paths contain keywords that help identify the
shapefile type:

- Point shapefiles contain `pts` or `point`.
- Line shapefiles contain `line`.

We use these keywords to create separate lists of point and line shapefiles.

```{r}
# Identify point shapefiles using their full file paths
pt_files = files[grep("pts|point", files, perl = TRUE)]

# Identify line shapefiles using their full file paths
ln_files = files[grep("line", files, perl = TRUE)]

# Count the number of files in each group
print(paste("Point shapefiles:", length(pt_files)))
print(paste("Line shapefiles:", length(ln_files)))
```

There should be **12 point shapefiles and 13 line shapefiles**.

The point shapefiles (`pt_files`) will be used in the following sections
to identify differences in column names and standardize the field data.

The line shapefiles (`ln_files`) are identified here but are not included
in the point-data integration workflow.


# 5. Examine Column Names in Point Shapefiles

Before combining the point shapefiles from different years, we need to examine
their attribute tables.

Each shapefile contains columns describing field observations, such as species,
vegetation cover, location, and environmental conditions. However, the column
names are not always consistent across years.

For example, two shapefiles may contain the same information but use different
column names. Some columns were also added in later years and are not present
in earlier datasets.

This section identifies these differences so we can determine which columns
need to be renamed, combined, or added when integrating the datasets.

**Important:** This section only examines column names. No changes are made
to the original shapefiles.


## 5.1 Extract Column Names from Each Shapefile

First, we create a table containing the column names from every point
shapefile.

For each shapefile, the code:

1. Opens the shapefile.
2. Extracts the year from its filename.
3. Gets the names of all columns.
4. Adds the year and column names to a combined table.

The resulting `pt_names` dataframe contains two columns:

- `year`: Year associated with the shapefile.
- `col_names`: Name of an attribute column in that shapefile.

Each row represents one column from one shapefile.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Create an empty dataframe to store column names
pt_names = data.frame()

# Loop through each point shapefile
for (i in seq_along(pt_files)) {

  # Read the shapefile
  dat = terra::vect(pt_files[i])

  # Get the filename without the folder path
  dat_name = basename(pt_files[i])

  # Find the location of the 4-digit year in the filename
  name_ind = regexpr("[0-9]{4}", dat_name)

  # Extract the year
  yr = as.numeric(substr(dat_name, name_ind, name_ind + 3))

  # Create a table containing the year and column names
  out = data.frame(
    year = yr,
    col_names = names(dat)
  )

  # Add the results to the combined table
  pt_names = rbind(pt_names, out)
}
```


## 5.2 Count How Often Each Column Name Appears

Next, we count how many times each column name appears across the point
shapefiles.

If a column name appears in all 12 shapefiles, it is consistently named
across the datasets.

If it appears in fewer than 12 shapefiles, there are several possible
explanations:

- The column has a different name in some years.
- The information was not collected in every year.
- The column was added or discontinued during the study.

This step helps identify columns that need further examination.

```{r}
# Count how many times each column name appears
colnames_count = pt_names %>%
  dplyr::count(col_names, name = "Count", sort = TRUE)

# Display the results as a table
knitr::kable(colnames_count)
```


The `Count` column indicates how many times each column name appears.

Because there are 12 point shapefiles, columns that appear in every
shapefile should have a count of 12.

**Note:** This assumes that each shapefile contains only one column
with a given name.


## 5.3 Identify Column Names Common to All Shapefiles

Some columns have the same name in every shapefile.

These columns do not need to be renamed before combining the datasets,
although their values may still require cleaning.

We identify these columns by selecting names that appear in all point
shapefiles.

```{r}
# Get the total number of point shapefiles
n_pt_files = length(pt_files)

# Identify column names found in every shapefile
cn_all = colnames_count %>%
  dplyr::filter(Count == n_pt_files) %>%
  dplyr::rename(Col_Name = col_names)

# Display the number of common columns
print(paste("There are", nrow(cn_all),
            "column names shared by all point shapefiles."))

# Display the common column names
knitr::kable(cn_all)
```


The resulting `cn_all` dataframe contains the names of columns shared
by all point shapefiles.

We will use these column names when creating the initial combined dataset
in Section 5.


## 5.4 Identify Column Names That Differ Between Shapefiles

Next, we identify columns that do not appear in every shapefile.

These columns require additional review to determine whether they:

- Contain the same information as another column with a different name.
- Were only collected in certain years.
- Are unnecessary for the final dataset.

```{r}
# Identify column names that are not shared by every shapefile
cn_missing = colnames_count %>%
  dplyr::filter(Count < n_pt_files) %>%
  dplyr::rename(Col_Name = col_names) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(Count))

# Display the number of inconsistent column names
print(paste("There are", nrow(cn_missing),
            "column names that are not shared by all point shapefiles."))

# Display the results
knitr::kable(cn_missing)
```


The resulting `cn_missing` dataframe contains columns that need to be
reviewed before combining the datasets.


## 5.5 Identify Columns That Are Not Needed

Some columns contain GPS metadata, processing information, or other
attributes that are not needed for the final analysis.

We create a list called `remove` containing these column names.

This list will help us distinguish unnecessary columns from columns that
need to be standardized.

**Important:** Creating this list does not delete any columns from the
original shapefiles.

```{r}
# Column names that are not needed in the final dataset
remove = c(
  "Easting", "Northing", "Datafile", "Feat_Name",
  "Corr_Type", "Filt_Pos", "GPS_Second", "GPS_Week",
  "Horz_Prec", "Max_PDOP", "Point_ID", "Unfilt_Pos",
  "Team", "Data_Dicti", "GNSS_Heigh", "Lifeform",
  "Max_HDOP", "Nutrient_I", "POINT_X", "POINT_Y",
  "Rcvr_Type", "Std_Dev", "Vert_Prec", "Treated"
)
```


## 5.6 Identify Columns That Still Need to Be Standardized

Now that we have identified unnecessary columns, we can remove their names
from the list of inconsistent columns.

This makes it easier to focus on columns that need to be renamed,
combined, or otherwise standardized.

The code below updates `cn_missing` by excluding column names listed
in `remove`.

**Note:** This only changes the list of column names. It does not
remove columns from the original shapefiles.

```{r}
# Remove unnecessary column names from the review list
cn_missing = cn_missing %>%
  dplyr::filter(!Col_Name %in% remove)

# Display the remaining columns that need to be reviewed
knitr::kable(cn_missing)
```


The remaining columns have been reviewed to determine how they should
be handled during data integration.

The following summarizes the standardization decisions.


### 5.6.1 Columns Added in Later Years

Some information was only collected in later years.

These columns should be retained in the combined dataset, with `NA`
(missing values) assigned to observations from years when the information
was not collected.

Columns include:

- `MatDensity`
- `Color`
- `Microsysti`
- `Canopy`
- Additional rake species and cover columns

These columns will be addressed in Section 5.


### 5.6.2 Position Within a Vegetation Patch

The columns `Position` and `PositionIn` describe where an observation
was collected within a vegetation patch.

However, different years use different column names and categories.

We will standardize the column name to `PositionIn`.

| Original value | Standardized value |
|---|---|
| Middle | Center |
| Center | Center |
| Start | StartEnd |
| End | StartEnd |
| Edge | StartEnd |
| StartEnd | StartEnd |
| NA | NA |

The final column will contain only `Center`, `StartEnd`, or `NA`.


### 5.6.3 Water Hyacinth Weevil Damage

Two column names were used to record water hyacinth weevil damage:

- `WH_Weevil_`
- `Weevil_dam`

These will be standardized to `WH_Weevil_Dam`.

The original columns contain slightly different categories.

The value `No` will be changed to `None`. Other existing categories,
including `Trace` and `Yes`, will be retained.


### 5.6.4 Photo Information

Photo information was recorded using several different column names:

- `Photos`
- `Link_Photo`
- `Photo`
- `Photo_Link`
- `Picture`

These will be combined into a single column called `Photo_Link`.

Some shapefiles contain more than one photo column. When this occurs,
we need to combine the information without losing existing values.


### 5.6.5 Comments

Comments were recorded in columns named `Comments` and `Comment`.

These will be combined into a single column called `Comments`.

When both columns are present, we need to account for values recorded
in either column.


### 5.6.6 Field Observation Assignment

Several columns describe how field observation locations were selected
or classified:

- `Preassigne`
- `Assignment`
- `newPatch`
- `Revisit_`

These will be combined into a single column called `Assignment`.

The final categories will be:

- `Random`
- `Revisit`
- `New`
- `NA`

Because the original columns use different combinations of `Yes`, `No`,
and categorical values, the appropriate corrections depend on which
columns were recorded together.

These rules will be applied in Section 5.

**Important:** Some combinations of the original values are ambiguous
and need to be reviewed before finalizing the assignment categories.


### 5.6.7 Flowering and Reproductive Status

Reproductive status was recorded using the following column names:

- `Reprodtive`
- `Flowering`
- `Spp1_Flowe`

These will be standardized into a single column called `Reproductive`.

For columns that record flowering as `Yes` or `No`:

- `Yes` will be changed to `Flowering`.
- `No` will remain `No`.

Other existing categories, such as `Budding`, will be retained.


### 5.6.8 SAV Adjacent to Water

Two columns were used to record whether SAV was adjacent to water:

- `SAV_adj_wa`
- `SAV_Adjace`

Both will be standardized to `SAV_adj_water`.


### 5.6.9 Rake Species and Cover

The rake sampling data contain species and cover measurements recorded
in alternating columns.

The original columns include `Rake_Spe1` through `Rake_Spe12`.

These will be standardized into species and cover columns:

- `Rake_Sp_1` through `Rake_Sp_6`
- `Rake_Sp_Cov_1` through `Rake_Sp_Cov_6`

Each species column will be paired with its corresponding cover column.

The rake cover values will also need to be converted from character
values to numeric values in Section 6.


## 5.7 Identify the Columns to Retain in the Final Dataset

Finally, we create a list of the columns intended for the cleaned dataset.

This list documents the information we want to retain after combining
and standardizing the shapefiles.

Some column names will be changed during the cleaning process, so this
list is a reference for the intended final dataset rather than a list
of columns that already exist.

```{r}
# Columns intended for the final cleaned dataset
final_cols = c(
  "ID", "GPS_Date", "GPS_Time",
  "Species_1", "Cover_1",
  "Species_2", "Cover_2",
  "Species_3", "Cover_3",
  "Species_4", "Cover_4",
  "Species_5", "Cover_5",
  "Cover_dry", "Cover_epi_", "Cover_wate",
  "Assignment", "Patch_Leng", "Patch_Widt",
  "Patch_Orie", "Location", "PositionIn",
  "MatDensity", "WH_Weevil_Dam", "Reproductive",
  "Color", "Canopy", "SAV_adj_water",
  "Secchi_Dep", "Secchi___B", "Microsysti",
  "Rake_Teeth", "Rake_Speci", "Rake_Spec2", 
  "Rake_Spec3", "Rake_Spec4", "Rake_Spec5", 
  "Rake_Spec6", "Rake_Spec7", "Rake_Spec8", 
  "Rake_Spec9", "Photo_Link", "Comments"
)
```

This completes the review of column names and identifies the
standardization rules needed to combine the datasets.

In Section 5, we will apply these corrections and create the combined
point dataset.


# 6. Combine Point Shapefiles into a Single Dataset

Now that we have identified differences in column names and values, we can
combine the point shapefiles into a single dataset.

We will first combine columns that are present in every shapefile. Then, we
will add columns that have different names across years, standardizing their
names and values as needed.

All changes are made to objects in R. The original shapefiles are not
modified or overwritten.

**Important:** The observations are combined in the order of `pt_files`.
When adding standardized columns, we must use the same file order so that
values are assigned to the correct observations.


## 6.1 Combine Columns Shared by All Shapefiles

We will start by combining columns that are present in every point shapefile.

Before combining the datasets, we need to ensure that they use the same
coordinate reference system (CRS). A CRS defines how geographic locations
are represented as coordinates.

The final dataset will use WGS84 / UTM Zone 10N (EPSG:32610).

The code below:

1. Opens each point shapefile.
2. Assigns a CRS if one is missing.
3. Reprojects the shapefile to EPSG:32610.
4. Keeps only columns shared by all shapefiles.
5. Adds the observations to a single combined SpatVector.

**Important — 2015 CRS needs verification:** The 2015 shapefile is missing
its CRS information. NAD83 / UTM Zone 10N is assumed because the 2014
shapefile was exported from Pathfinder with this CRS. However, the 2015
data may actually use WGS84 / UTM Zone 10N. The 2015 dataset should
either be re-exported from Pathfinder with its correct CRS information
or its original CRS verified.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Get the column names shared by all point shapefiles
start_cols = unique(cn_all$Col_Name)

# Create an empty SpatVector to store the combined observations
dat = terra::vect()

# Loop through each point shapefile
for (i in seq_along(pt_files)) {

  # Read the original shapefile
  d = terra::vect(pt_files[i])

  # IMPORTANT - 2015 CRS NEEDS VERIFICATION
  # The 2015 shapefile is missing its CRS information.
  # NAD83 / UTM Zone 10N is assumed because the 2014 shapefile was
  # exported from Pathfinder with this CRS.
  #
  # The 2015 data may actually use WGS84 / UTM Zone 10N instead.
  # The file should be re-exported from Pathfinder with its correct
  # CRS information, or the original CRS should be verified.

  if (terra::crs(d) == "") {
    terra::crs(d) = "EPSG:26910"
  }

  # Reproject all shapefiles to WGS84 / UTM Zone 10N
  d = terra::project(d, "EPSG:32610")

  # Keep only columns that are present in every shapefile
  d_out = d %>%
    dplyr::select(dplyr::all_of(start_cols))

  # Add observations to the combined dataset
  dat = rbind(dat, d_out)
}

# Display the number of observations and columns
dim(dat)
```


The resulting `dat` object is a `SpatVector` containing observations
from all point shapefiles.

At this stage, it only contains columns shared across every shapefile.
Additional columns will be added in the following sections.


## 6.2 Standardize Comments Columns

Field comments were recorded using different column names:

- `Comments`
- `Comment`

We want all comments stored in one column called `Comments`.

Some shapefiles contain both columns. When this occurs, we will retain
the existing `Comments` value and use `Comment` to fill missing values.

If neither column contains a value, the observation will have `NA`.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Create an empty vector to store comments from all shapefiles
comments = vector()

# Loop through each point shapefile
for (i in seq_along(pt_files)) {

  # Read the shapefile
  d = terra::vect(pt_files[i])

  # Start with missing values for all observations
  comment = rep(NA_character_, nrow(d))

  # Use values from the Comments column, if it exists
  if ("Comments" %in% names(d)) {
    comment = as.character(d$Comments)
  }

  # Treat empty strings as missing values
  comment[!is.na(comment) & trimws(comment) == ""] = NA

  # Use Comment to fill missing values in Comments
  if ("Comment" %in% names(d)) {

    comment2 = as.character(d$Comment)
    comment2[!is.na(comment2) & trimws(comment2) == ""] = NA

    # Find rows where Comments is missing but Comment has a value
    missing = which(is.na(comment) & !is.na(comment2))

    # Fill missing comments
    comment[missing] = comment2[missing]
  }

  # Add comments from this shapefile to the combined vector
  comments = c(comments, comment)
}

# Add the standardized Comments column to the combined dataset
dat$Comments = comments
```


**Note:** If both columns contain different, nonmissing comments for the
same observation, this rule retains the value from `Comments`. These
cases should be reviewed if both entries may contain useful information.


## 6.3 Standardize Water Hyacinth Weevil Damage Columns

Water hyacinth weevil damage was recorded using two different column names:

- `WH_Weevil_`
- `Weevil_dam`

Both columns describe weevil damage and will be combined into a single
column called `WH_Weevil_Dam`.

The original datasets also use slightly different categories:

| Original value | Standardized value |
|---|---|
| No | None |
| None | None |
| Trace | Trace |
| Yes | Yes |
| NA | NA |

The value `No` will be changed to `None`. All other values will be retained.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Create an empty vector to store weevil damage observations
WH_Weevil_Dam = vector()

# Loop through each point shapefile
for (i in seq_along(pt_files)) {

  # Read the shapefile
  d = terra::vect(pt_files[i])

  # Find the column containing weevil damage information
  x = grep("Weev", names(d), ignore.case = TRUE)

  # Extract the values if the column exists
  if (length(x) == 1) {

    wh = as.character(terra::values(d[, x])[[1]])

  } else if (length(x) == 0) {

    # Assign missing values if no weevil damage column exists
    wh = rep(NA_character_, nrow(d))

  } else {

    # Stop if multiple matching columns are found
    stop(paste("Multiple weevil damage columns found in:",
               basename(pt_files[i])))
  }

  # Standardize No to None
  wh[wh == "No"] = "None"

  # Add values to the combined vector
  WH_Weevil_Dam = c(WH_Weevil_Dam, wh)
}

# Add the standardized column to the combined dataset
dat$WH_Weevil_Dam = WH_Weevil_Dam
```


## 6.4 Standardize Photo Columns

Photo information was recorded using several different column names:

- `Photos`
- `Link_Photo`
- `Photo`
- `Photo_Link`
- `Picture`

We want to combine these into one column called `Photo_Link`.

Most shapefiles contain only one photo column. However, the 2023
shapefile contains two photo columns.

When multiple photo columns are present, we will retain values from
the first column and use the remaining columns to fill missing values.

If no photo column exists, the observation will receive `NA`.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Create an empty vector to store photo information
Photo_Link = vector()

# Loop through each point shapefile
for (i in seq_along(pt_files)) {

  # Read the shapefile
  d = terra::vect(pt_files[i])

  # Find columns containing photo information
  x = which(names(d) %in%
              c("Photos", "Link_Photo", "Photo", "Photo_Link", "Picture"))

  # Start with missing values for all observations
  pl = rep(NA_character_, nrow(d))

  # Combine values from any photo columns found
  if (length(x) > 0) {

    for (j in x) {

      # Get values from the current photo column
      photo = as.character(terra::values(d[, j])[[1]])

      # Treat empty strings as missing values
      photo[!is.na(photo) & trimws(photo) == ""] = NA

      # Fill missing values without overwriting existing photo information
      missing = which(is.na(pl) & !is.na(photo))
      pl[missing] = photo[missing]
    }
  }

  # Add photo information to the combined vector
  Photo_Link = c(Photo_Link, pl)
}

# Add the standardized Photo_Link column to the combined dataset
dat$Photo_Link = Photo_Link
```

**Note:** If an observation contains different, nonmissing photo values
in multiple columns, this code retains the first value encountered.
Additional photo information would need to be handled separately if
multiple photos should be preserved.


## 6.5 Standardize Position Within a Vegetation Patch

The columns `Position` and `PositionIn` describe where an observation
was collected within a vegetation patch.

Different years use different names and categories. We will combine
these into one column called `PositionIn`.

The standardized values will be `Center`, `StartEnd`, and `NA`.

| Original value | Standardized value |
|---|---|
| Middle | Center |
| Center | Center |
| Start | StartEnd |
| End | StartEnd |
| Edge | StartEnd |
| StartEnd | StartEnd |
| NA | NA |

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Create an empty vector to store position information
PositionIn = vector()

# Loop through each point shapefile
for (i in seq_along(pt_files)) {

  # Read the shapefile
  d = terra::vect(pt_files[i])

  # Find the position column
  x = which(names(d) %in% c("Position", "PositionIn"))

  # Extract values if the column exists
  if (length(x) == 1) {

    pos = as.character(terra::values(d[, x])[[1]])

  } else if (length(x) == 0) {

    # Assign NA if no position column exists
    pos = rep(NA_character_, nrow(d))

  } else {

    # Stop if both columns exist and need to be combined
    stop(paste("Multiple position columns found in:",
               basename(pt_files[i])))
  }

  # Standardize position categories
  pos[pos == "Middle"] = "Center"
  pos[pos %in% c("Start", "End", "Edge")] = "StartEnd"

  # Add values to the combined vector
  PositionIn = c(PositionIn, pos)
}

# Add the standardized column to the combined dataset
dat$PositionIn = PositionIn
```


## 6.6 Standardize Field Observation Assignment

Different years used different columns to describe how field observation
locations were selected or classified.

These include:

- `Preassigne`
- `Assignment`
- `newPatch`
- `Revisit_`

We want to combine these into one column called `Assignment`.

The final categories are `Random`, `Revisit`, `New`, and `NA`.

The appropriate correction depends on which original column was used.
In some years, `Preassigne` and `newPatch` were recorded together and
must be interpreted as a pair.

**Important:** One of the rules below is provisional and needs group
review. It is marked clearly in the code so it can be revisited later.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Create an empty vector to store assignment categories
Assignment = vector()

# Loop through each point shapefile
for (i in seq_along(pt_files)) {

  # Read the shapefile
  d = terra::vect(pt_files[i])

  # Find assignment-related columns
  cn = names(d)[names(d) %in%
                  c("Preassigne", "Assignment", "newPatch", "Revisit_")]

  # Start with missing values for all observations
  a = rep(NA_character_, nrow(d))

  # Case 1: Only one assignment-related column exists
  if (length(cn) == 1) {

    a = as.character(terra::values(d[, cn])[[1]])

    # Revisit_ uses Yes/No to indicate revisit status
    if (cn == "Revisit_") {
      a[a == "No"] = "Random"
      a[a == "Yes"] = "Revisit"
    }

    # Preassigne indicates whether a location was randomly preassigned
    if (cn == "Preassigne") {
      a[a == "No"] = NA
      a[a == "Yes"] = "Random"
    }

    # newPatch indicates whether the observation was a new patch
    if (cn == "newPatch") {
      a[a == "No"] = NA
      a[a == "Yes"] = "New"
    }
  }

  # Case 2: Both Preassigne and newPatch exist
  if (all(c("Preassigne", "newPatch") %in% cn)) {

    pa = as.character(d$Preassigne)
    np = as.character(d$newPatch)

    # New patch that was not randomly preassigned
    a[pa == "No" & np == "Yes"] = "New"

    # PROVISIONAL RULE - NEEDS GROUP REVIEW
    # Preassigne = No and newPatch = No is assigned "Revisit".
    # These observations were not randomly preassigned and were not
    # new patches. They are assumed to be revisits, but their actual
    # assignment type is uncertain.
    # This rule may need to be changed to NA.
    a[pa == "No" & np == "No"] = "Revisit"

    # Randomly preassigned observations
    a[pa == "Yes" & np == "Yes"] = "Random"
    a[pa == "Yes" & np == "No"] = "Random"

    # Not preassigned, with missing newPatch information
    a[pa == "No" & is.na(np)] = "Revisit"
  }

  # Stop if an unexpected combination of columns is found
  if (length(cn) > 1 &&
      !setequal(cn, c("Preassigne", "newPatch"))) {

    stop(paste("Unexpected assignment columns in:",
               basename(pt_files[i])))
  }

  # Add values to the combined vector
  Assignment = c(Assignment, a)
}

# Add the standardized Assignment column to the combined dataset
dat$Assignment = Assignment
```

The provisional assignment rule has been retained from your original
workflow. It should be reviewed with the research group before the
dataset is considered final.


## 6.7 Standardize Flowering and Reproductive Status

Reproductive status was recorded using different column names:

- `Reprodtive`
- `Flowering`
- `Spp1_Flowe`

These will be combined into one column called `Reproductive`.

Some years recorded reproductive status as `Yes` or `No`, while others
used more descriptive categories such as `Flowering` or `Budding`.

We will change `Yes` to `Flowering` and retain the other categories.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Create an empty vector to store reproductive status
Reproductive = vector()

# Loop through each point shapefile
for (i in seq_along(pt_files)) {

  # Read the shapefile
  d = terra::vect(pt_files[i])

  # Find the reproductive status column
  x = which(names(d) %in%
              c("Reprodtive", "Flowering", "Spp1_Flowe"))

  # Extract values if the column exists
  if (length(x) == 1) {

    rep_status = as.character(terra::values(d[, x])[[1]])

  } else if (length(x) == 0) {

    rep_status = rep(NA_character_, nrow(d))

  } else {

    stop(paste("Multiple reproductive status columns found in:",
               basename(pt_files[i])))
  }

  # Standardize Yes to Flowering
  rep_status[rep_status == "Yes"] = "Flowering"

  # Add values to the combined vector
  Reproductive = c(Reproductive, rep_status)
}

# Add the standardized column to the combined dataset
dat$Reproductive = Reproductive
```


## 6.8 Standardize SAV Adjacent to Water Columns

Two column names were used to record whether SAV was adjacent to water:

- `SAV_adj_wa`
- `SAV_Adjace`

Both will be standardized to `SAV_adj_water`.

The original values will be retained.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Create an empty vector to store SAV adjacency observations
SAV_adj_water = vector()

# Loop through each point shapefile
for (i in seq_along(pt_files)) {

  # Read the shapefile
  d = terra::vect(pt_files[i])

  # Find the SAV adjacency column
  x = grep("SAV_adj", names(d), ignore.case = TRUE)

  # Extract values if one matching column exists
  if (length(x) == 1) {

    sav = terra::values(d[, x])[[1]]

  } else if (length(x) == 0) {

    sav = rep(NA, nrow(d))

  } else {

    stop(paste("Multiple SAV adjacency columns found in:",
               basename(pt_files[i])))
  }

  # Add values to the combined vector
  SAV_adj_water = c(SAV_adj_water, sav)
}

# Add the standardized column to the combined dataset
dat$SAV_adj_water = SAV_adj_water
```


## 6.9 Standardize Rake Species and Cover Columns

Rake sampling data contain species names and their corresponding percent
cover values.

The rake columns always follow the same order:

1. `Rake_Teeth`: Number of rake teeth.
2. First species name.
3. Percent cover of the first species.
4. Second species name.
5. Percent cover of the second species.
6. Continue alternating species and cover columns.

Most years contain up to five species and their corresponding cover
values. Two years contain a sixth species and cover measurement.

The original column names are not consistent with the intended final
names, so we will rename them based on their position.

For example:

| Original column | Standardized column |
|---|---|
| Rake_Teeth | Rake_Teeth |
| Rake_Speci | Rake_Sp_1 |
| Rake_Spec2 | Rake_Sp_Cov_1 |
| Rake_Spec3 | Rake_Sp_2 |
| Rake_Spec4 | Rake_Sp_Cov_2 |
| ... | ... |
| Rake_Spec11 | Rake_Sp_6 |
| Rake_Spec12 | Rake_Sp_Cov_6 |

We will add missing rake columns as `NA` for years when fewer species
were recorded.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Create a list to store rake data from each shapefile
rake_list = vector("list", length(pt_files))

# Standardized rake column names
rake_cols = c(
  "Rake_Teeth",
  paste0("Rake_Sp_", 1:6),
  paste0("Rake_Sp_Cov_", 1:6)
)

# Loop through each point shapefile
for (i in seq_along(pt_files)) {

  # Read the shapefile
  d = terra::vect(pt_files[i])

  # Find rake columns in their original order
  x = grep("rake", names(d), ignore.case = TRUE)

  # Extract rake attributes as a dataframe (without geometry)
  rake_dat = as.data.frame(d[, x])

  # Rename the first column
  names(rake_dat)[1] = "Rake_Teeth"

  # Identify alternating species and cover columns
  species_cols = seq(2, ncol(rake_dat), 2)
  cover_cols = seq(3, ncol(rake_dat), 2)

  # Rename species columns
  names(rake_dat)[species_cols] =
    paste0("Rake_Sp_", seq_along(species_cols))

  # Rename cover columns
  names(rake_dat)[cover_cols] =
    paste0("Rake_Sp_Cov_", seq_along(cover_cols))

  # Add missing rake columns for years with fewer species
  for (col in rake_cols) {
    if (!col %in% names(rake_dat)) {
      rake_dat[[col]] = NA
    }
  }

  # Keep rake columns in the same order for every year
  rake_dat = rake_dat[, rake_cols]

  # Store this year's rake data
  rake_list[[i]] = rake_dat
}

# Combine rake data from all years
rake = do.call(rbind, rake_list)

# Remove the original rake columns from the combined dataset
x = grep("rake", names(dat), ignore.case = TRUE)

if (length(x) > 0) {
  dat = dat[, -x]
}

# Add the standardized rake columns
for (col in names(rake)) {
  dat[[col]] = rake[[col]]
}
```

**Note:** The rake cover values may still contain percent signs. These
will be removed and converted to numeric values in Section 6.


## 6.10 Add Columns That Were Only Collected in Certain Years

Some attributes were only collected in later years and are therefore
missing from earlier shapefiles.

These include:

- `MatDensity`
- `Color`
- `Microsysti`
- `Canopy`

We want to retain these attributes in the combined dataset.

For years when an attribute was not collected, its values will be `NA`.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Create empty vectors to store the additional attributes
MatDensity = vector()
Color = vector()
Microsystis = vector()
Canopy = vector()

# Loop through each point shapefile
for (i in seq_along(pt_files)) {

  # Read the shapefile
  d = terra::vect(pt_files[i])

  # Mat density
  x = grep("MatDensity", names(d), ignore.case = TRUE)

  if (length(x) == 1) {
    md = terra::values(d[, x])[[1]]
  } else {
    md = rep(NA, nrow(d))
  }

  # Color
  x = grep("Color", names(d), ignore.case = TRUE)

  if (length(x) == 1) {
    col = terra::values(d[, x])[[1]]
  } else {
    col = rep(NA, nrow(d))
  }

  # Microcystis
  x = grep("Microsysti", names(d), ignore.case = TRUE)

  if (length(x) == 1) {
    mi = terra::values(d[, x])[[1]]
  } else {
    mi = rep(NA, nrow(d))
  }

  # Canopy
  x = grep("Canopy", names(d), ignore.case = TRUE)

  if (length(x) == 1) {
    ca = terra::values(d[, x])[[1]]
  } else {
    ca = rep(NA, nrow(d))
  }

  # Add values to the combined vectors
  MatDensity = c(MatDensity, md)
  Color = c(Color, col)
  Microsystis = c(Microsystis, mi)
  Canopy = c(Canopy, ca)
}

# Add the standardized columns to the combined dataset
dat$MatDensity = MatDensity
dat$Color = Color
dat$Microsystis = Microsystis
dat$Canopy = Canopy
```


**Check the combined dataset**

Before proceeding to Section 6, check that the combined dataset contains
the expected number of observations and that the standardized columns
were added correctly.

```{r}
# Display the number of observations and columns
dim(dat)

# Display the column names
names(dat)

# Check the standardized assignment categories
table(dat$Assignment, useNA = "ifany")

# Check the standardized position categories
table(dat$PositionIn, useNA = "ifany")

# Check reproductive status categories
table(dat$Reproductive, useNA = "ifany")
```

The combined `dat` object is now ready for the final cleaning steps in
Section 6, including converting percent-cover values to numeric,
replacing missing-value codes, and renaming ambiguous columns.



# 7. Clean Up the Final Dataset

Now that the point shapefiles have been combined and their attributes
standardized, we need to make a few final corrections.

This section will:

1. Assign a unique ID to each observation.
2. Arrange columns in a consistent order.
3. Convert percent-cover values from character to numeric.
4. Replace -99 (a missing-data code) with NA.
5. Rename abbreviated columns to make their meanings clearer.
6. Check the final dataset before exporting it.

All changes are made to the combined dataset in R. The original
shapefiles are not modified.


## 7.1 Assign Unique IDs and Reorder Columns

The original shapefiles may contain observation IDs that repeat across
years. We will assign each observation a new, unique ID in the combined
dataset.

We will also arrange the columns so that related information appears
together, such as species observations, vegetation cover, environmental
conditions, and rake sampling data.

The column order does not affect the spatial data or analysis results,
but it makes the attribute table easier to navigate.

```{r}
# Assign a unique ID to each observation in the combined dataset
dat$ID = seq_len(nrow(dat))

# Specify the desired column order
col_order = c(
  "ID", "GPS_Date", "GPS_Time",
  "Species_1", "Cover_1",
  "Species_2", "Cover_2",
  "Species_3", "Cover_3",
  "Species_4", "Cover_4",
  "Species_5", "Cover_5",
  "Cover_dry", "Cover_epi_", "Cover_wate",
  "Location", "PositionIn", "Assignment",
  "Patch_Leng", "Patch_Widt", "Patch_Orie",
  "SAV_adj_water", "Depth_to_S", "Secchi_Dep",
  "Secchi___B", "Microsystis", "MatDensity",
  "WH_Weevil_Dam", "Reproductive", "Canopy", "Color",
  "Rake_Teeth",
  "Rake_Sp_1", "Rake_Sp_Cov_1",
  "Rake_Sp_2", "Rake_Sp_Cov_2",
  "Rake_Sp_3", "Rake_Sp_Cov_3",
  "Rake_Sp_4", "Rake_Sp_Cov_4",
  "Rake_Sp_5", "Rake_Sp_Cov_5",
  "Rake_Sp_6", "Rake_Sp_Cov_6",
  "Photo_Link", "Comments"
)

# Check whether any expected columns are missing
missing_cols = setdiff(col_order, names(dat))

if (length(missing_cols) > 0) {
  stop(paste("Missing expected columns:",
             paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", ")))
}

# Reorder columns while keeping the spatial geometry
dat_ord = dat[, col_order]

# Display the dimensions of the reordered dataset
dim(dat_ord)
```


**Note:** This check deliberately stops the script if an expected column is missing rather than silently creating or removing fields. This helps identify problems introduced during data integration.


## 7.2 Convert Percent-Cover Columns to Numeric

Several vegetation cover columns contain percentages stored as
character values (text), such as `"25%"` or `"100%"`.

These values need to be converted to numeric values before they can
be used in calculations or statistical analyses.

We will remove the percent sign (`%`) and convert the remaining value
to numeric.

For example:

| Original value | Cleaned value |
|---|---|
| `"25%"` | 25 |
| `"50%"` | 50 |
| `"100%"` | 100 |
| `NA` | NA |

The resulting values remain on a scale of 0–100, not 0–1.

We use `mutate()` and `across()` to apply the correction to all columns
beginning with `Cover_`.

```{r}
# Convert vegetation percent-cover columns from character to numeric
dat_cor = dat_ord %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    dplyr::across(
      dplyr::starts_with("Cover_"),
      ~ as.numeric(stringr::str_remove(as.character(.x), "%"))
    )
  )
```

The `mutate()` function modifies the selected columns while retaining
all other attributes and the spatial geometry.


## 7.3 Replace Missing-Value Codes with NA

Some numeric fields use `-99` to indicate that a measurement was
not collected or was unavailable.

In R, missing values should be represented by `NA` rather than `-99`.

If we leave `-99` in these columns, R may treat it as a real
measurement, which could affect calculations and statistical analyses.

We will replace `-99` with `NA` in:

- `Depth_to_S`: Depth to submerged aquatic vegetation.
- `Secchi_Dep`: Secchi depth.
- `Rake_Teeth`: Number of rake teeth.

```{r}
# Replace -99 with NA in the depth and rake measurements
dat_cor$Depth_to_S[dat_cor$Depth_to_S == -99] = NA

dat_cor$Secchi_Dep[dat_cor$Secchi_Dep == -99] = NA

dat_cor$Rake_Teeth[dat_cor$Rake_Teeth == -99] = NA
```

Only the specified columns are modified. Other values are retained.


## 7.4 Convert Rake Species Cover to Numeric

The rake species cover columns also contain percentages stored as
character values.

These columns begin with `Rake_Sp_Cov_`.

As with the vegetation cover columns, we will remove the percent sign
and convert the values to numeric.

```{r}
# Convert rake species percent-cover columns to numeric
dat_cor = dat_cor %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    dplyr::across(
      dplyr::starts_with("Rake_Sp_Cov_"),
      ~ as.numeric(stringr::str_remove(as.character(.x), "%"))
    )
  )
```

The resulting values remain on a 0–100 scale.


## 7.5 Rename Abbreviated Columns

Some original column names were abbreviated because shapefiles have
a 10-character limit for attribute field names.

Now that the datasets have been combined, we can use more descriptive
names to make the attributes easier to understand.

For example:

- `Patch_Leng` becomes `Patch_Length`.
- `Secchi_Dep` becomes `Secchi_Depth`.
- `WH_Weevil_Dam` becomes `WH_Weevil_Dam` (already standardized).

Instead of renaming columns by their numerical positions, we will
rename them using their existing names. This is safer because it does
not depend on the order of columns in the dataset.

```{r}
# Create the final dataset
dat_final = dat_cor

# Rename abbreviated columns
names(dat_final)[names(dat_final) == "Cover_epi_"] = "Cover_epi_algea"
names(dat_final)[names(dat_final) == "Cover_wate"] = "Cover_water"

names(dat_final)[names(dat_final) == "Patch_Leng"] = "Patch_Length"
names(dat_final)[names(dat_final) == "Patch_Widt"] = "Patch_Width"
names(dat_final)[names(dat_final) == "Patch_Orie"] = "Patch_Orientation"

names(dat_final)[names(dat_final) == "Depth_to_S"] = "Depth_2_SAV"
names(dat_final)[names(dat_final) == "Secchi_Dep"] = "Secchi_Depth"
names(dat_final)[names(dat_final) == "Secchi___B"] = "Secchi_Bottom"

names(dat_final)[names(dat_final) == "MatDensity"] = "WH_MatDensity"
names(dat_final)[names(dat_final) == "Reproductive"] = "FAV_Reproductive"
names(dat_final)[names(dat_final) == "Canopy"] = "FAV_Canopy"
names(dat_final)[names(dat_final) == "Color"] = "FAV_Color"
```

These changes only affect column names. The values within the columns
are not modified.


## 7.6 Check the Final Dataset

Before exporting the cleaned data, we should check that the columns
have the expected names and data types.

This is an important quality-control step because it helps identify
unexpected results from the cleaning process.

```{r}
# Convert the attribute table to a dataframe for inspection
# This does not modify the original SpatVector
test = as.data.frame(dat_final)

# Display the structure of the final attribute table
str(test)

# Display the final column names
names(dat_final)

# Check the number of observations and columns
dim(dat_final)
```

We can also confirm that the percent-cover columns are numeric.

```{r}
# Identify all vegetation and rake cover columns
cover_cols = grep(
  "^Cover_|^Rake_Sp_Cov_",
  names(test),
  value = TRUE
)

# Display the data type of each cover column
sapply(test[, cover_cols, drop = FALSE], class)
```

All selected cover columns should now have a numeric data type.


## 7.7 Export the Cleaned Dataset

Once the final dataset has been checked, it can be saved for future
analyses.

Because the standardized column names exceed the 10-character limit
of shapefiles, we will use a GeoPackage (`.gpkg`) instead.

GeoPackages support longer column names, spatial geometry, and
attribute data in a single file.

The cleaned dataset will be saved outside the raw-data directory.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Set the output file location
output_gpkg = file.path(outpath, "all_field_pts.gpkg")

# Export the cleaned SpatVector as a GeoPackage
terra::writeVector(
  dat_final,
  output_gpkg,
  filetype = "GPKG",
  overwrite = TRUE
)
```

**Note:** This chunk has `eval=FALSE`, meaning it will not run
automatically when the R Markdown document is knitted.

Once the dataset has been reviewed and approved, remove `eval=FALSE`
to enable the export.


# 8. Outstanding Tasks and Data Verification

The point shapefiles have been combined and standardized, but several
issues still need to be verified before the dataset is considered final.

This section documents known uncertainties, decisions that still need to
be made, and additional quality-control checks.

**Important:** Some of these issues may require corrections to the original
data exports or changes to the cleaning rules in Sections 5 and 6.
Do not directly edit or overwrite the original raw shapefiles.

## 8.1 Verify the Coordinate Reference System of the 2015 Dataset

- [ ] **Verify the original CRS of the 2015 point shapefile.**

The 2015 shapefile was exported without coordinate reference system (CRS)
information. In Section 5.1, NAD83 / UTM Zone 10N (EPSG:26910) was
assigned because the 2014 shapefile was exported from GPS Pathfinder
using this CRS.

However, the 2015 dataset may actually use WGS84 / UTM Zone 10N
(EPSG:32610).

**Action needed:**
- Re-export the 2015 dataset from GPS Pathfinder with the correct CRS
  information, or verify the CRS using the original export settings.
- If necessary, update the CRS assignment in Section 5.1.
- Rerun the data integration workflow after correcting the CRS.

## 8.2 Review the Provisional Assignment Rules

- [ ] **Confirm how to classify observations where `Preassigne = No`
  and `newPatch = No`.**

In Section 5.6, these observations are currently classified as `Revisit`.

This rule was not established by the research group and is based on the
following interpretation:

- `Preassigne = No`: The location was not randomly preassigned.
- `newPatch = No`: The observation was not collected at a new patch.

Therefore, the observation was assumed to be a revisit.

However, the correct category may be `Revisit` or `NA` if the type of
visit cannot be determined.

**Action needed:**
- Discuss this rule with the research group.
- Determine whether `Revisit` is an appropriate classification.
- Update Section 5.6 if the group decides to use a different rule.

- [ ] **Review the related rule for `Preassigne = No` and missing
  `newPatch` values.**

These observations are also currently classified as `Revisit` in
Section 5.6. Confirm whether this interpretation is appropriate when
new-patch status was not recorded.

## 8.3 Verify GPS Time Values and Standardize Time Format

The `GPS_Time` column requires additional quality control before the
dataset is finalized.

### 8.3.1 Check for Incorrect GPS Times

- [ ] **Identify observations with GPS times outside approximately
  7:00 AM to 5:00 PM.**

Field observations were generally collected between approximately
7:00 AM and 5:00 PM.

Times outside this range may indicate that the GPS receiver clock or
time settings were not handled correctly when the data were exported
from GPS Pathfinder.

**Action needed:**
- Examine `GPS_Time` values across all years.
- Identify observations with times earlier than 7:00 AM or later than
  approximately 5:00 PM.
- Determine which original shapefiles contain potentially incorrect times.
- Reprocess and re-export affected datasets from GPS Pathfinder using
  the correct time settings.
- Rerun the integration workflow with the corrected files.

**Note:** Times outside the expected range should be flagged for review,
not automatically changed or deleted. They may indicate an export issue,
but the original records need to be checked.

### 8.3.2 Decide on a Standard GPS Time Format

- [ ] **Select a consistent time format for `GPS_Time`.**
- [ ] **Confirm the time zone used in the original GPS exports.**

The final dataset should use a consistent time format across all years.

Decisions still needed:

- **Clock format:** 12-hour (AM/PM) or 24-hour.
- **Time zone:** UTC or Pacific Time.
- **Time zone documentation:** If Pacific Time is selected, account for
  Pacific Standard Time (PST) and Pacific Daylight Time (PDT).

**Action needed:**
- Verify how GPS Pathfinder recorded and exported the original times.
- Decide on the standard format and time zone.
- Add code to Section 6 to standardize `GPS_Time`.
- Document the final time format and time zone in the dataset metadata.


## 8.4 Verify Combined Comments and Photo Information

- [ ] **Review observations with values in multiple comment columns.**

Section 5.2 combines `Comments` and `Comment`, prioritizing `Comments`
when both columns contain values.

Confirm whether this priority is appropriate and whether any observations
contain different, useful comments in both columns.

- [ ] **Review observations with multiple photo fields.**

Section 5.4 combines photo information from several differently named
columns.

When multiple photo columns contain values, the current code retains
the first nonmissing value.

Confirm whether any observations contain multiple distinct photo
references that should be preserved.

## 8.5 Verify the Final Dataset Before Release

- [ ] **Confirm that all observations were retained during integration.**

Compare the total number of observations in the original point shapefiles
with the number of observations in the final combined dataset.

- [ ] **Verify standardized categorical values.**

Check that the final `PositionIn`, `Assignment`, `WH_Weevil_Dam`, and
`Reproductive` columns contain the intended categories.

- [ ] **Verify rake species and cover columns.**

Confirm that species names and their corresponding percent-cover values
are correctly paired, particularly for the two years containing six
rake species.

- [ ] **Check numeric fields and missing values.**

Confirm that percent-cover columns are numeric and that missing-value
codes such as `-99` have been handled appropriately.

- [ ] **Finalize column names and dataset documentation.**

Review the final column names, definitions, units, and categorical
values before preparing metadata and distributing the cleaned dataset.
